content: In the absence of antiretroviral therapy (ART), more than half of HIV-infected infants progress to AIDS and die by the age of two. However, initiating ART in early life presents several challenges. These include the potential for drug resistance due to prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs, limited drug options, uncertain dosing for some medications, and concerns about long-term toxicities. Key decisions in managing HIV in young children involve determining the optimal time to start ART, selecting the appropriate drug regimen, and deciding whether to substitute drugs or interrupt therapy at any point. This review evaluates the following: (1) the timing of ART initiation in children under three years of age, (2) the choice of ART regimen, specifically comparing non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens with protease inhibitor (PI)-based regimens, and (3) alternative strategies to optimize ART, such as induction-maintenance therapy (starting with four drugs and then reducing to three), substituting PIs with NNRTIs after achieving virological suppression, or interrupting ART. A systematic search of databases identified 735 unique studies, of which only eight met the inclusion criteria. These studies addressed the timing of ART initiation (n=2), the choice of initial regimen (n=3), substitution of lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) with nevirapine (NVP) (n=1), induction-maintenance strategies (n=1), and treatment interruption (n=1). One trial with sufficient statistical power demonstrated that initiating ART in asymptomatic infants with good immunological status reduced the risk of mortality or disease progression by 75% (HR=0.25; 95% CI 0.12–0.51; p=0.0002). However, a smaller pilot trial found no significant difference in CD4 cell counts between early and deferred treatment groups after 12 months of ART. Children starting ART with an NVP-based regimen had a 1.79-fold higher risk of treatment failure at 24 weeks compared to those starting with an LPV/r-based regimen (95% CI 1.33–2.41; p=0.0001). This increased risk was observed regardless of prior NVP exposure for PMTCT. Similarly, the risk of virological failure at 24 weeks was 1.84 times higher for children on NVP-based regimens compared to LPV/r-based regimens (95% CI 1.29–2.63; p=0.0008). The difference in virological outcomes was more pronounced when ART was initiated within the first year of life. In infants who started on an LPV/r-based regimen and achieved sustained virological suppression, substituting LPV/r with NVP after a median of nine months reduced the likelihood of virological failure (defined as a viral load >50 copies/mL) compared to those who remained on LPV/r (HR=0.62; 95% CI 0.41–0.92; p=0.02). However, the risk of confirmed virological failure at a higher viral load (>1000 copies/mL) was significantly greater in children who switched to NVP (HR=10.19; 95% CI 2.36–43.94; p=0.002). An induction-maintenance strategy using a four-drug NNRTI-based regimen for 36 weeks, followed by a three-drug regimen, resulted in greater CD4 cell count increases at 36 weeks (mean difference 1.70; 95% CI 0.61–2.79; p=0.002) and better viral load suppression at 24 weeks (OR 1.99; 95% CI 1.09–3.62; p=0.02) compared to standard three-drug NNRTI-based ART. However, these benefits were short-term, and the strategy is not recommended for routine use. One trial on treatment interruption, which compared continuous ART from infancy with interrupted ART, was terminated early because most infants had interruptions lasting less than three months. Children in the treatment interruption group had similar growth and rates of serious adverse events as those in the continuous ART group. In conclusion, initiating ART in asymptomatic children under one year of age reduces morbidity and mortality. However, the clinical benefits of starting ART in asymptomatic children aged 1–3 years remain unclear. Evidence supports the use of LPV/r-based regimens as the first-line treatment over NVP-based regimens, regardless of PMTCT exposure. New formulations of LPV/r are urgently needed to facilitate implementation of WHO recommendations. Substituting LPV/r with NVP after achieving virological suppression appears promising but may be challenging without routine viral load monitoring. The induction-maintenance approach offers short-term benefits but lacks sustained advantages and is not recommended. Treatment interruption following early ART initiation is impractical in settings where close monitoring is not feasible.
